question:
(a) Explain why the electrical conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor is higher than that of an insulator but lower than that of a metal.
(b) Using the concept of energy gap, explain why the conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor increases with temperature.

options.A:
(a) In metals the conduction band is partially filled or overlaps the valence band, giving many free carriers. Insulators have a large forbidden gap and almost no thermally excited carriers. Intrinsic semiconductors have a small gap, so their conductivity lies between metals and insulators.
(b) As temperature rises, more electrons gain enough energy to cross the small band gap and create electron-hole pairs. The increased carrier concentration raises intrinsic-semiconductor conductivity.
options.B:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor has greater conductivity than a metal because it has no band gap.
(b) Temperature reduces the number of electron-hole pairs and therefore raises resistance only.
options.C:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor is an insulator because its energy gap is infinite.
(b) Its conductivity is independent of temperature.
options.D:
(a) Metals, insulators and semiconductors have identical energy gaps.
(b) Heating destroys all charge carriers in a semiconductor.
